extracted.intended_audience: researchers, academics, journal editors, research-integrity officers, students and general readers interested in scientific integrity
extracted.subtask_description: Compilation of standards, types, and examples of research misconduct and problematic scholarly practices in academic publishing (plagiarism, data fabrication/falsification, authorship/peer-review manipulation, ethics violations, retractions). Uses case examples and editorial/institutional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Copying others' text or ideas without attribution; a grounds for retraction, investigation, and sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the text include multiple journal publications retracted (e.g., Roques had 13 articles retracted) and high-profile cases (e.g., Karl-Theodor zu Guttenberg's doctoral dissertation revoked). The CNRS report described regularly 'bad scholarly practices' and 'active negligence'. Plagiarism findings often lead to retractions, revocation of degrees, resignation, or other sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Reusing one's own previously published material without appropriate disclosure or citation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Bruno Frey admitted to multiple acts of self-plagiarism in articles about the Titanic, calling them 'grave mistake[s]'. Self-plagiarism can result in retractions and reputational sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data fabrication and falsification
rubrics_metrics.description: Making up data (fabrication) or altering/manipulating data/results (falsification) to misrepresent findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly named as research misconduct (e.g., Ranga P. Dias found to have committed data fabrication and falsification; Victor Ninov, Jan Hendrik Schön, Diederik Stapel, Marc Hauser, etc.). Consequences include paper retractions, dismissal, institutional and funder sanctions, and criminal or civil penalties in severe cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image manipulation / doctored figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Altering images or presenting duplicated/flipped images to misrepresent experimental results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Lönnstedt's study included images that appeared to duplicate specimens and flipped images to make fish counts appear larger; such manipulations led to retraction. Image manipulation is treated as falsification and can prompt formal investigation and retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship misconduct (inappropriate authorship, adding names improperly)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improperly adding, omitting, or claiming authorship (e.g., adding one's name post-submission or claiming undeserved credit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Ashok Pandey added his name to papers he edited and then handled peer review, violating journal policies; this resulted in dozens of retractions. Authorship misconduct undermines authorship transparency and can trigger retraction and institutional action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-review manipulation (fake or compromised peer review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Manipulating the peer-review process, including faking reviewer identities or handling one's own review to secure publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page documents large-scale cases of 'fake peer reviews' and authors faking emails to do their own peer review, leading to many retractions (Retraction Watch examples). Journals respond with retractions and corrections when peer-review manipulation is discovered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to properly document and preserve research results
rubrics_metrics.description: Not maintaining adequate records, raw data, or materials necessary to verify and reproduce reported findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Brian Wansink was found to have 'failure to properly document and preserve research results' among other failings; lack of documentation hinders verification and may lead to retraction or expressions of concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problematic statistical techniques and misreporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Using inappropriate statistical methods or misreporting data/analyses in ways that mislead about the results' validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited in the Wansink case ('problematic statistical techniques, misreporting of research data') and other examples where flawed analysis contributed to retractions. Journals and institutions scrutinize statistical appropriateness during misconduct inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics-approval violations and human/animal-ethics breaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to obtain, report, or follow required ethics approvals for research involving humans or animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Didier Raoult and other researchers had papers retracted for ethics violations; journals can retract papers and institutions may impose sanctions when ethical approvals are missing or misconduct in ethics oversight is found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-reproducibility / replication failure as red flag
rubrics_metrics.description: Results that cannot be reproduced in independent replication efforts, which may indicate flawed, fraudulent, or irreproducible research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: James Cook University studies on coral reef fish showed 100% replication failure, triggering formal investigation. Systematic replication failures prompt scrutiny, informal and formal investigations, and potential retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship/publication record fabrication (falsified CVs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Falsely claiming publications or fabricating a record of scholarly output on curricula vitae or applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mart Bax was found to have never published 61 papers he listed on his CV. Fabricated publication records can lead to institutional disciplinary action, retractions of claimed works, and loss of positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideologically biased, unethical, or scientifically flawed research
rubrics_metrics.description: Research that is unethical or scientifically defective, including work based on racist or agenda-driven premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Philippe Rushton's research was described as 'unethical, scientifically flawed, and based on racist ideas and agenda.' Such fundamental deficiencies can lead to retraction and professional censure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large-scale authorship/peer-review/authorship-manipulation schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Coordinated networks that manipulate authorship, peer review, or reviewer identities to produce multiple fraudulent publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Springer Nature retracted 58 papers from seven journals for 'authorship manipulation, peer-review manipulation, and/or plagiarism'; institutional and publisher investigations may uncover systemic schemes and prompt mass retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial remedies: retraction, expression of concern, correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals use formal notices—retraction, expression of concern, correction—to signal problems with the published record and to correct the literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page repeatedly documents use of retractions, expressions of concern, and corrections (e.g., counts of retractions for many individuals). These are the standard editorial mechanisms for addressing confirmed or suspected misconduct or honest errors.
